solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, mirror symmetry); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Militias react badly, hunting for goods? (13)

indicatorNotes.badly: Something done badly comes out wrong, so the letters of MILITIAS REACT end up in a jumbled order.

annotation.surface: Armed irregulars bungling a looting raid.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a playful definition: someone always hunting for goods is obsessed with possessions.
annotation.definitionFit: A materialistic person puts acquiring possessions above everything, forever on the lookout for more goods.

entries.clue: Not inclined to anger this person, European king (4)

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
K = king, as in chess notation

annotation.surface: A mild-mannered European monarch who won't lose his temper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'This person' in a clue usually means the setter, so it gives ME.
annotation.definitionFit: A meek person is gentle and submissive, slow to take offence or flare up.

entries.clue: Sorry to ignore outsiders in shelter in downpour (7)

indicatorNotes.to ignore outsiders: Ignoring a word's outsiders means leaving off its first and last letters, so SORRY becomes ORR.
indicatorNotes.in: One thing in another sits inside it, so ORR goes inside TENT.

blocks.note: SORRY without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: Apologising for leaving people out in the rain while you shelter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sorry' reads as an apology in the surface; here it is just letter material.
annotation.definitionFit: A torrent is a violent, heavy flow, and it is used of rain coming down in sheets.

entries.clue: Proportion of allowance cut short (5)

indicatorNotes.cut short: A word cut short loses its final letter, so the allowance word drops its last letter.

blocks.note: a fixed daily allowance of food, as issued to soldiers

annotation.surface: A share of someone's allowance being trimmed.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'proportion of allowance' as one phrase; 'Proportion' is the definition and 'of' only links it to the wordplay. RATION loses its N.
annotation.definitionFit: A ratio expresses one quantity as a proportion of another.

entries.clue: Charge account, copper’s, initially exceeded (6)

indicatorNotes.initially: Initially means at the start, so only the first letter of 'exceeded' is taken.

blocks.note: AC is the abbreviation for account
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

annotation.surface: A police officer's account of a speeding charge.
annotation.walkthrough: In the surface, copper means a police officer; here it is the metal, Cu. The apostrophe S is used as a letter of its own.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the legal sense: formally blaming someone for an offence.

entries.clue: Go-between’s re-entry, aim I’d worked on (12)

indicatorNotes.worked on: Letters that are worked on get reshaped, so RE-ENTRY AIM I'D is rearranged.

annotation.surface: A negotiator's plan for getting back in, which they've been working on.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S after 'Go-between' stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: An intermediary acts between two parties, carrying messages or negotiating for them.

entries.clue: Extra item to some extent characteristic (5)

indicatorNotes.to some extent: To some extent means partly, so only part of the phrase 'Extra item' is used.

annotation.surface: Adding one more item is somewhat typical behaviour.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the gap between the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A trait is a distinguishing characteristic of a person or thing.

entries.clue: Following authorisations, beer event with nothing left at finish? (9,4)

annotation.definition: event with nothing left at finish?

indicatorNotes.Following: One thing following another comes after it, so ALE goes after CLEARANCES.

annotation.surface: After getting permits, a beer festival where every barrel is drained by the end.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition sounds like a drinking session that finishes the beer; it describes a shop selling off all its stock.
annotation.definitionFit: A clearance sale sells off all remaining stock, so ideally nothing is left when it finishes.

entries.clue: Abnormal feature of Montserrat I cited (7)

indicatorNotes.feature of: A feature of something is part of it, so the answer is found inside the words that follow.

annotation.surface: Someone citing an unusual characteristic of the Caribbean island Montserrat.
annotation.walkthrough: Montserrat is a small British territory in the Caribbean; the answer spans three words.
annotation.definitionFit: Erratic behaviour is irregular, departing from the normal pattern.

entries.clue: Mock afternoon meals, old-time ultimately (5)

indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter of 'old-time' is taken.

blocks.note: afternoon tea is a light British meal

annotation.surface: Poking fun at old-fashioned afternoon teas.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Mock' could be an adjective going with 'afternoon meals'; it is the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: poking fun at someone, usually good-naturedly.

entries.clue: Evil one’s betrayer, we hear, one with something to show (12)

indicatorNotes.we hear: What we hear is sound, so the answer is spelt the way the phrase is said.

annotation.surface: Denouncing the traitor who serves the devil.
annotation.walkthrough: The two words run together when spoken to give one long word.
annotation.definitionFit: A demonstrator shows how a product or procedure works.

entries.clue: Pleasant wish, ready-made? Not entirely, resort needed (8)

indicatorNotes.Not entirely: Not entirely means not all of it, so READY-MADE loses its last letter.
indicatorNotes.resort: To re-sort is to sort again, so the remaining letters are rearranged.

annotation.surface: Hoping a wish comes true off the shelf, though a holiday resort is needed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Resort' looks like a holiday destination; read it as re-sort, to sort again.
annotation.definitionFit: A daydream is a pleasant fantasy, often of something wished for.

entries.clue: Strongly criticise extremely abject course taken (6)

indicatorNotes.extremely: Extremely means at the extremes, so only the outer letters of 'abject' are taken.

blocks.note: first and last letters of abject
a tack is a course taken, as by a sailing boat

annotation.surface: Laying into a thoroughly miserable way of going about things.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' reads as intensifying 'abject'; it selects the ends of that word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the verbal sense, as when a reviewer lays into a play or a policy.

entries.clue: Talk about headgear supplier (7)

blocks.note: a hatter makes or sells hats

annotation.surface: Gossip concerning a hat seller.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Talk about' looks like a phrase; 'Talk' is the definition and 'about' gives C.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, leaning to the idle, rapid, trivial kind of conversation.

entries.clue: Referring to a child’s motive (6)

blocks.note: re means regarding, as in a letter heading

annotation.surface: Asking about a child's motive.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe S reads as possessive in the surface but stands for 'is', linking wordplay to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A reason is the motive or cause behind an action.

entries.clue: Metal tool earns no praise at first in new arrangement (7)

indicatorNotes.at first: At first points to the start of each word, so 'no praise' gives N and P.
indicatorNotes.new arrangement: A new arrangement puts letters in a different order, so EARNS N P are rearranged.

blocks.note: first letters of no and praise

annotation.surface: A tool that gets no thanks in a reorganised workshop.
annotation.walkthrough: A spanner is the British word for a wrench.
annotation.definitionFit: A spanner is a metal hand tool for gripping and turning nuts and bolts.

entries.clue: Determined foolish talk must change finally (6)

indicatorNotes.must change finally: Changing a word finally means swapping its final letter, so the L of DRIVEL becomes another letter.

annotation.surface: A resolve that silly chatter has to stop sooner or later.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue does not say which letter replaces the L; the definition decides it, since only DRIVEN means determined.
annotation.definitionFit: A driven person is determined and highly motivated.

entries.clue: In the end, sad article suggests couple lose hope (7)

indicatorNotes.In the end: The end of a word is its last letter, so the last letters of sad, article and suggests are taken.

blocks.note: last letters of saD, articlE, suggestS

annotation.surface: A gloomy newspaper piece hints that a couple have given up on their relationship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In the end' seems to apply only to 'sad', giving D; it covers the next three words, and 'article' is not a grammatical article here.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb for giving up every expectation that things will improve.

entries.clue: They’re usually in cinemas, small things to munch (5)

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

annotation.surface: Popcorn and snacks, the small things people munch in a cinema.
annotation.walkthrough: The snacks look like the answer to 'usually in cinemas'; they are the wordplay, and the definition points to the seating.
annotation.definitionFit: Seats fill a cinema auditorium; the definition is a descriptive phrase rather than a synonym.

entries.clue: Proletariat held back, somewhat annoyed (5)

indicatorNotes.held back: Back means reading from right to left, so the letters are taken in reverse order.
indicatorNotes.somewhat: Somewhat means partly, so only part of 'Proletariat' is used.

annotation.surface: The working class, kept in check, are growing irritated.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat annoyed' seems to be the definition, but 'somewhat' is the part-of-word signal and 'annoyed' alone defines.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, though stronger than mild irritation: really angry.

entries.clue: Law that’s no longer strictly accurate (5)

blocks.note: an act of parliament is a law

annotation.surface: A statute that has been repealed and so no longer quite applies.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'no longer strictly accurate' as one phrase, but the break comes after 'no longer'; ex- is the prefix for former, as in ex-wife.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: precise in every detail, with no rounding or approximation.

entries.clue: New red van in front of a gallery (7)

indicatorNotes.New: Something made new is remade, so the letters of RED VAN are rearranged.
indicatorNotes.in front of: One thing in front of another comes first, so the rearranged letters precede A.

annotation.surface: A brand-new red van parked outside an art gallery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Gallery' suggests art; here it means a roofed open platform along a house.
annotation.definitionFit: A veranda is a roofed gallery or porch running along the outside of a building.

entries.clue: Note race error (8)

blocks.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale
a sprint is a short race

annotation.surface: A memo pointing out a mistake in a race result.
annotation.walkthrough: The three words read as a phrase; each is a separate part, with the definition last.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the specific kind of mistake made in typesetting or printing.

entries.clue: Genuine regret comes after time (4)

indicatorNotes.comes after: Something that comes after another is placed behind it, so RUE follows T.

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time

annotation.surface: Real remorse only arrives with time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Genuine regret' reads as one phrase; 'Genuine' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: real and authentic, as in a true friend or a true copy.
